in_context.text: Paul is closing his appeal for Onesimus, the servant who had left Philemon and become a believer. He has asked Philemon to receive Onesimus as a brother and offered to pay any debt himself. Here he says he wrote because he is sure Philemon will respond well, and will even go beyond what Paul asks.

speaker.text: Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, writing with Timothy. He signs part of the letter in his own hand.

audience.text: Philemon, Paul's dearly beloved fellow-worker. The letter also greets Apphia, Archippus, and the church that met in his house.

affected.text: Onesimus, Philemon's servant, whom Paul calls his son and is sending back.

what.text: Paul states his confidence that Philemon will obey his request and do more than Paul has asked. The verse does not say what that 'more' would be.

events.text: Onesimus had left Philemon, met Paul, and become a believer. Paul is now sending him back with this letter.

written.text: Traditional: about AD 60-62, during Paul's imprisonment in Rome. Scholarly: nearly all accept Paul wrote it, but some place the imprisonment at Ephesus (about AD 54-55) or Caesarea (about AD 57-59).

where.text: Paul wrote from prison, though the letter does not name the city. It was sent to Philemon's house church, traditionally placed at Colossae.

purpose.text: Paul ends his appeal with warm confidence rather than pressure. Earlier he said he could command but chose to ask for love's sake, wanting Philemon's kindness to be willing, not forced.

big_picture.text: Paul often tells churches he has confidence in them, that they will do what is right. This verse follows that same pattern of trust in fellow believers.

for_readers.text: The verse shows that faith works out in love that goes beyond the minimum asked. Paul trusts Philemon's love, which he praised at the start of the letter, to carry him further than the request.

why_it_matters.text: The word's root meaning is to persuade; here it is glossed 'having been persuaded of.' Paul's confidence is a settled conviction about Philemon.
The word means obedience. Yet in this letter Paul chose to beseech rather than command (1:8-9), and wanted Philemon's kindness to be willing, "not as it were of necessity" (1:14).
The word means over, above, or beyond. Paul expects Philemon to go beyond what he has written.

takeaway.text: Paul trusts that love will move Philemon to welcome Onesimus generously, even past what was asked. Christian kindness at its best is willing, not forced.

resolved.reason: The lexicon lists 2 Corinthians 7:15 and 10:6 under obedience 'in general' (with a subjective genitive), not under obedience to God. It says nothing about 'apostolic teaching'. The claim misstates how the cited source classifies these uses.
resolved.fix: claim rewritten to match its sources
